Photo: Clay LeConey/Unsplash (CC0)

In today’s edition: homelessness in the United States fell by over 6% in 2025, the FDA has approved a low-cost generic HIV prevention shot, and biologists are restoring mangroves in Mexico with the help of an unexpected ally: crocodiles.

US homelessness sees biggest decline in more than a decade
After years of rising numbers and record highs, homelessness in the United States fell by more than 6% in 2025, representing approximately 49,000 fewer people without stable housing. This marks the second consecutive year of decline, following a smaller decrease in 2024.

Source: NPR

Minnesota announces that the state has effectively ended veteran homelessness
Ramsey County is now the final community in the state to meet the required benchmarks. It does not mean that no veterans are experiencing homelessness or that it will never happen again, but it does mean that Minnesota now has a statewide system designed to quickly connect veterans who lose their housing with stable accommodation, typically within a few months.

Source: KSTP/ABC

FDA approval of low-cost generic HIV prevention shot aims to widen access
The US Food and Drug Administration has approved a generic version of lenacapavir, the only HIV-prevention injection administered twice a year. The decision will expand access to affordable HIV prevention, potentially making the drug available more quickly and at lower cost across 120 low- and middle-income countries.

Source: AP News

Sierra Leone reports 32% drop in maternal deaths in one year

A 300-day campaign aims to eliminate preventable maternal and child deaths and reach children who have never received a vaccine. With 226 days completed, preliminary results point to meaningful progress. More than 10,000 previously unvaccinated children have received vaccines, maternal deaths have fallen by more than 32%, and child deaths have declined by 12.3% compared with the 2005 baseline.

Source: GAVI

World's largest liquid-energy storage goes online in China
The facility in Qinghai began generating electricity on October 30th, making it the world’s largest grid-connected LAES project. It offers 10 hours of continuous power output, creating a foundation for renewable energy integration alongside domestically developed tech.

Source: PV Magazine
